title: Recombinant venom proteins in insect seminal fluid reduce female lifespan
one_line: Engineered Drosophila males expressing venom proteins in their accessory glands transfer them in seminal fluid and shorten the lifespan of mated females, a proof of concept for a same-generation 'Toxic Male Technique' of genetic biocontrol.
key_claims: Of 7 venom proteins tested in Drosophila melanogaster, two shortened mated female lifespan: Γ-CNTX-Pn1a (spider) by 37% and δ-AITX-Avd2a (sea anemone) by 64%.
Effect strength increased with higher male:female ratios in mating assays.
Modelling of Aedes aegypti control programs predicted TMT gives 40–60% greater reduction in blood feeding than current genetic biocontrol methods.
Modelled effectiveness rose with higher release ratios, higher female remating rates, and lower density-dependent mortality.
Selected venoms target insect ion channels, with the authors reporting no effect on mammals/vertebrates, and the system is self-limiting without continued releases.
limitations: Proof of concept is only in Drosophila melanogaster; no demonstration in target pest or vector species such as Aedes aegypti.
Mosquito impact estimates come from computer simulation, not experiments.
Venom expression levels and conditional (inducible) expression systems are not yet optimised or built.
Integration with existing sterilisation methods remains untested.
Long-term ecological impacts, resistance evolution, cost at scale, and regulatory pathway are unresolved.
open_questions: Does venom expression in male accessory glands reduce female lifespan and blood feeding in Aedes aegypti under cage and field conditions?
Can conditional expression keep engineered males fit and mating-competitive enough for mass release?
How quickly would resistance to venom-targeted insect ion channels arise in wild populations?
